newsitem.title: ITALY: TENNIS-CORRETJA PUTS CLAY RUN DOWN TO COACH.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-CORRETJA PUTS CLAY RUN DOWN TO COACH.

text.p: When Alex Corretja raced to the side of the court after winning the Italian Open tennis title on Sunday, it was not to embrace his watching girlfriend. It was to hug his coach.
The biggest single reason for Corretja's outstanding form on clay this season - just four defeats in 26 matches - is the return of his childhood coach, Javier Duarte.

Thoughout his triumphant week in Rome, Corretja has consistently dedicated his rise up the rankings to Duarte, who coached him from age of 11 until he was 18 and who has been working with him again since the beginning of the year.
The results have been astonishing. Sunday's 7-5 7-5 6-3 win over Marcelo Rios of Chile in Rome was the fourth clay court final for Corretja this year.
The Spaniard beat compatriot Francisco Clavet in Estoril in April to end a three-year spell in which he failed to lift an ATP tour title.

In the same month, he lost in straight sets to Mark Philippoussis in Munich and to Rios in the Monte Carlo final in another three-setter, a defeat from which he said he had emerged mentally strengthened.
"Mentally I really improved (since Monte Carlo). I was much better than Rios today," he said.
"Before I was working hard but was not that focused. In the tournaments I was not that concentrated. Now I'm more professional than before and that's why I'm playing better," the Spaniard said.

The decision to change coach followed an epic four-hour battle with Pete Sampras in the quarter-finals of the U.S. Open last year in which the world number one was physically sick on a Corretja match point but went on to win the game.
"When I lost that match I thought 'why can't I play like that every week'," Corretja said. "I changed coaches and it gave me confidence. I saw that my game was improving a lot."
Corretja, 23, said his Italian victory was the most important of his career and gave him hope of going on to win a Grand Slam title.
"I've won two good tournaments before but not like this. It's unbelievable to win here. The next step will be to win a Grand Slam," he said.
And with the French Open a week away, Corretja's impressive form on clay gives him a chance of doing just that.
The Barcelona-born player's ability to keep the ball in play has brought him more clay court wins than any other player this year but, not content with this, he also has ambitions on other surfaces.

"Now my game is more aggresive than before. I'm serving and returning better. I used to have fear of going to the net. Now If I have to go, I go," he said. "I learnt to play on hard courts and now let's see what happens on grass."

But clay remains Corretja's domain and with compatriots Albert Costa, who won in Barcelona last month, Australian Open finalist Carlos Moya and Sergi Bruguera he is expected to do well at Roland Garros.
Until now the least known of the top Spaniards, he may finally generate some media attention at home after shooting into the world's top 10 for the first time with Sunday's win.
"In Spain if you're top 15 it's not good enough. I've been working so hard but even in Barcelona nobody knows me," he said.
